new_statements.rule_in_words: Khamti is a syllable-tone language (five citation tones; every syllable, including each syllable of polysyllabic loans, carries a tone). No source states where word stress falls. The only prosodic asymmetry described is reduction of non-final syllables: the first element of disyllabic compounds may be 'abbreviated' to C+ə with a 'subdued pitch' (Manpoong's depress tone), and Morey (2005: 133, 196; 2005b: 166) reports that the revised Khamti script reserves a tone mark for 'unstressed syllables in polysyllabic loan words'. This implies full (tone-bearing) final syllables versus reducible pre-final syllables, but no author formulates a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (Pali, Assamese, Burmese, English): every syllable receives a tone, mostly Tone 1 (Das p.54); Morey 2005: 133 reports for the closely related Phake that unstressed medial syllables of Pali loans take the level first tone and that the Khamti script has a special mark for such unstressed syllables. Weidert 1977: 28 notes 'toneless syllables' realised at mid pitch with relaxed vowel articulation.
new_statements.domain_note: All statements concern lexical/citation forms and the syllable as tone-bearing unit; Morey 2005: 81 explicitly says word/phrase-level prosodic (stress) analysis was not undertaken for the Tai languages of NE India. Das describes Indian Khamti (Chongkham, Arunachal Pradesh); Inglis 2014 (Myanmar Khamti) likewise says only 'tone with every syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Das 2014, Handique 2016, Borgohain 2019 and Borah 2020 describe Indian Tai-Khamti (Chongkham/Namsai area, Arunachal Pradesh, and Narayanpur, Assam); Inglis 2014 and Dockum 2017/2019 describe Khamti of Myanmar ('Khamti Shan', Chindwin/Putao). All fall under kham1290; Glottolog lists sub-dialects but none of the sources is keyed to a dialect glottocode, and the tone systems reported for India (Harris/Morey/Das) and Myanmar (Inglis) match (five tones).

sources.locator: Ch. II, sec. 2.8 p. 53 (tone on every syllable) and sec. 2.6.2 p. 45 (depress tone on abbreviated syllables)
sources.note: Ch. II (pp. 31-55) covers consonants, vowels, five citation tones, syllable structure and morphophonology. p.53: every syllable is marked by tone; loanwords get a tone on every syllable (mostly Tone 1). p.45 (after Manpung 1993): 'Depress tone: subdued pitch for abbreviated syllable' -- reduced CV(ə) first syllables of compounds (məD-muŋ2 'mango') take a subdued pitch. The word 'stress' is never applied to Khamti; no statement of where word stress falls. Variety: Tai-Khamti of Chongkham/Namsai, Lohit district, Arunachal Pradesh.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 Khamti (p.166): tone box after Harris 1976 / Manpoong 1993 / own recordings; 'Tone marks 1 & 2 are reserved for unstressed tones, and 8 & 9 for certain prosodic emphasis.' Nothing on where stress falls.

sources.citation: Weidert, Alfons. 1977. Tai-Khamti phonology and vocabulary. (Beiträge zur Südasienforschung 27.) Wiesbaden: Franz Steiner. 92 pp.
sources.note: Stratificational treatment of monosyllable phonology: vowels, consonants, five tones (pp. 19-20). Only prosodic remark, p.28: 'No attempt has been made to give a morphophonological interpretation of toneless syllables; their phonetic realization usually ranges in a mid-tone height between the high and low tones together with a rather relaxed vowel articulation.' No word-stress statement (confirms the earlier scan's suspicion).

sources.citation: Handique, Sunil. 2016. A critical study of the morphology of Khamti language. PhD thesis, Dibrugarh University. (Shodhganga 10603/367059)
sources.note: Sec. 2.7.5 Tone (pp. 57-60): five lexical tones (Praat); quotes Manpoong New Tai Reader Standard I p. IX: depress tone-symbol used when a consonant+ə is 'pronounced singly in subdued pitch as preceding phoneme of abbreviated syllable of compound word'; author adds 'Tone 1 and 2 are stress less or natural tone'. No placement rule.

sources.citation: Inglis, Douglas. 2014. This here thing: Specifying morphemes an3, nai1, and mai2 in Tai Khamti reference-point constructions. PhD dissertation, University of Alberta.
sources.note: Sec. 2.4.1 (pp. 35-36): Tai languages incl. Khamti 'have tone with every syllable and very little tone sandhi'; 'Each syllable bears a single tone' (five tones, high level 55 the most frequent). Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the dissertation. Variety: Khamti of Myanmar (Khamti Shan).

sources.citation: Morey, Stephen. 2005. The Tai languages of Assam - a grammar and texts. Pacific Linguistics 565. Canberra: ANU. 438 pp.
sources.note: Khamti phonology treated only via Harris 1976 and Weidert 1977 (pp. 54-57; tones, vowels). p.81: 'In the present study of the Tai languages of Northeast India, the level of prosodic analysis undertaken by Noss [stress, intonation, rhythm] has not been possible and remains an area for further research.' p.133 and p.196: in Chau Khouk Manpoong's revised Khamti script 'Tone mark No. 2 is used for unstressed syllables in polysyllabic loan words, while Nos. 8 and 9 are used for prosodic purposes'. No statement of stress placement.
